title: The Treaty on Open Skies: Potential Lessons for International AI Agreements
full_text:
“Potentially the most important measure to build confidence ever undertaken”.

— U.S. Secretary of State, James A. Baker, on the Open Skies Treaty.1

Summary

The Treaty on Open Skies (1992, entered force 2002) allowed 25 signatory states — the US, Russia, Canada, and 22 European nations — to conduct short-notice surveillance flights over each others’ territories to monitor for military buildup. These flights used aircraft with limited-capability sensors, and all raw data and mission reports were available to all signatories. After successful operation for many years, the US withdrew from the treaty in 2020, followed by Russia in 2021.

This article analyses the Open Skies negotiations to identify potential lessons for developing international AI agreements. Particularly, as a verification agreement, it draws lessons that could inform AI verification, and examines contentious issues in negotiation that may be relevant for AI governance negotiations in the future. While contextual differences may limit the applicability of these lessons, insights from Open Skies can provide valuable guidance for navigating similar challenges in AI agreement development.

Key findings

There are several structural treaty elements of Open Skies which led to its success. These are:

Short-notice overflights (72 hours notice), giving the ability to ensure military buildup was not occurring, while ensuring overflown states could take action on particularly sensitive matters.

Overflight access to the entire territory of signatories, providing confidence that secretive military buildup was not occurring in any part of a signatory’s territory.

Cooperative certification events for aircraft and sensors. Since many states were present and involved in certification events, states could be confident that aircraft and their sensors did not have capabilities beyond those agreed in Open Skies.

Equality of sensors, meaning all treaty parties were subject to the same restricted sensors, and no party received extra advantages that would incentivise withholding overflight data.

Pre-flight inspections of aircraft were available if requested, ensuring no changes were made to aircraft, and sensors had not been hidden.

Cooperation during missions between overflying and overflown states, easing the inspection process, and ensuring proper protocols were followed.

Detailed missions reports containing key inspection findings sent to all signatory states after each inspection, signed-off by the overflown state.

Availability of all raw mission data, upon request by signatories.

Some cost-sharing, including aircraft-sharing and sensor-sharing from better-resourced states, or pooling of resources by smaller states, and reimbursement by the overflying state to the overflown state for mission expenses.

The creation of the Open Skies Consultative Commission (OSCC): a treaty body with a representative from each signatory state to resolve disputes and make future decisions about Open Skies. The commission operated on the basis of consensus, and met at least four times per year.

Middle powers can be decisive facilitators in negotiations. Canada played a crucial role in Open Skies. They organised and fully funded the first Open Skies conference, worked tirelessly with the US and other states to move negotiations forward, and invited European nations to join the first conference. Other middle powers also played very significant roles in negotiations, with states like Hungary, Romania, Finland, and Sweden successfully challenging the positions of superpowers.

Commitment from a major power is essential. Open Skies only came to fruition because in 1989 President Bush made it a priority for the US. If the US had not fully engaged in pursuing discussions with the USSR and Russia with the help of Canada and other nations, Open Skies likely would have failed. The Bush-Gorbachev summit in 1990 revived Open Skies and brought significant progress.

Equality and proportional treatment can be inevitable negotiation endpoints. The US and USSR spent years fighting for advantages over each other — sensor superiority, intelligence asymmetries, and territorial restrictions, with little progress. Middle powers primarily wanted equality from the start. The US realised negotiations would not move forward unless there was equality with the USSR. The final treaty included equal sensor capabilities, sensor-sharing, universal data access and flight quotas that were proportional to territorial area.

Domestic and geopolitical factors play a significant role in shaping negotiations. Different incentives drove states’ behaviours in important ways. The US revived Open Skies to actively respond to a changing geopolitical climate, while the Soviets were much more open to Open Skies under Gorbachev’s Glasnost (transparency) policy. Canada wanted to be more influential in European politics, so they paid for the first conference and continued to push forward negotiations, while other European powers wanted access to shared aircraft and advanced US sensors, pushing for equality of sensors.

States may resist intrusive verification when they perceive unfair treatment and distrust. Verification can be intrusive. Open Skies required states to accept short-notice overflights across their entire territories, which was a particularly sensitive demand for the secretive USSR. Such intrusive verification is resisted when states think that there is unfair treatment or reasons for distrust. For example, early proposals allowing the US and UK to use superior sensors only heightened distrust among participants. Negotiations moved forward when this perception was addressed through fairness in joint certification of aircraft and sensors, standardised sensor capabilities, shared inspection data, and direct coordination between host and overflying states.

Establishing shared goals before establishing mechanisms could accelerate negotiations. While Open Skies participants quickly agreed that overflights would be the treaty's primary verification mechanism, they struggled to agree on the treaty's underlying goals. Negotiators found themselves hotly debating specific provisions — sensor-sharing arrangements, data access protocols, and flight quotas — without first clarifying why these mechanisms served the treaty's purpose. Progress only accelerated after states became aligned on fundamental goals, suggesting that goal-setting should precede detailed mechanism design. Though such disagreements are common in negotiations, prioritising agreement on goals while maintaining technical awareness of implementation may be more efficient than negotiating goals and mechanisms simultaneously.

Different negotiation formats serve different purposes, and all can be useful. While the formal negotiation format used in Ottawa was valuable for understanding states' initial positions, it left no room for informal discussions where more entrenched positions could be resolved. Success only came after incorporating a mix of approaches: formal negotiations, informal talks, leader-to-leader meetings, allied discussions, and prenegotiations. The 1990 Bush-Gorbachev summit exemplifies this — the leaders made substantial progress on Open Skies, effectively reigniting negotiations. Similarly, allied discussions allowed blocs like NATO to coordinate their positions and bring draft proposals into formal negotiations for consideration.

Costs can play a significant part in confidence-building agreements. Open Skies experienced recurring funding disputes over aircraft, sensors, operational expenses, and personnel. Russia ratified the treaty largely because costs were comparable to alternative intelligence-gathering methods. Resource-constrained middle powers sought shared aircraft and sensors because they couldn't afford them independently. These cost disputes proved highly contentious and required years of negotiation through the OSCC to resolve.

How to navigate this article

Introduction provides context for examining Open Skies as a potential model for AI verification agreements and explains the treaty's basic framework.

The history of Open Skies traces the treaty's evolution from Eisenhower's 1955 proposal through Bush's 1989 revival, the four negotiation rounds (1990-1992), and eventual collapse following US and Russian withdrawals in 2020-2021.

Contentious issues in negotiation examines five major disputes that significantly shaped negotiations and treaty outcomes.

Lessons learned synthesises nine key insights from the treaty's three-decade success that could inform other international agreements.

Introduction

Verification has emerged as a central concern in recent international AI governance discussions.2 This growing focus on verification infrastructure reflects recognition that effective international AI governance requires credible oversight capabilities to build trust between nations. Open Skies’ aerial inspection regime offers a relevant historical precedent for designing verification that balances transparency and security concerns.

What is the Treaty on Open Skies?

The Treaty on Open Skies was signed in 1992 by the United States, Canada, Russia, and 22 European nations.3 It allows each signatory state short-notice overflights over the entire territory of other signatories in order to collect data relevant to the buildup of military activities, such as the detection of vehicles, artillery, and aircraft. The sensors used for data collection are limited in capability.4 Data is openly available to other signatories via mission reports, and raw data can be easily obtained by signatories.5 Open Skies was also able to be used for verification of other agreements, such as the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe (CFE).6

The key features of the final version of the treaty7 were:

Sensors: Only certain radar and optical sensors are allowed. Notably, signals intelligence (i.e. intercepting communications or other signals during overflights) is not allowed.8 All sensors are calibrated within agreed capabilities.9

Aircraft: The host state can choose to provide aircraft. Otherwise, the overflying state can use certified aircraft they own, or those owned by another signatory state.10

Notice period: There is a 72 hour notice period before flights, and further time-based protocols around submitting flight paths and other aspects.11

Quotas: Agreed flight quotas specify how many times a state is to be inspected each year, and are based loosely on territory size.12

All signatory territories are open to inspection: The entire territory of signatories is open to overflights, with flight paths only to be denied for safety or logistical reasons (not security, secrecy, or other reasons).13

Data: Mission reports are sent to all signatories within seven days after an overflight.14 All raw data is available at the cost of sharing.15

Decision-making: The Open Skies Consultative Commission (OSCC) was formed to resolve issues and meets at least four times per year, operating on consensus.16

Treaty accession: Other states would be allowed to join Open Skies.17

Around 1,500 flights occurred under Open Skies before the United States left the treaty in 2020, over accusations of Russia’s violations of the treaty. The US upheld their decision in 2021 under Biden.18 Russia left in 2021, claiming the US was no longer interested in arms control.19

The history of Open Skies

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BTdi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8fefb475-7b70-4762-bd8d-e55b8dfd9573_2432x1498.png]]

This history contains three parts: Origins: 1955-1990; Negotiations: 1990-1992; and Implementation and decline: 1992-2021.

Origins: 1955-1990

The idea of reconnaissance overflights between the Soviet Union and the US was first proposed by Dwight D. Eisenhower’s administration in 1955, but received little interest from the Soviets at the time. Eisenhower's motivation for proposing Open Skies is disputed — he may have genuinely sought to reduce tensions through mutual transparency given Soviet military secrecy, or alternatively aimed to expose Soviet unwillingness to negotiate. The proposal failed when the Soviets quickly rejected it as an espionage plot. The Soviets later showed some interest to avoid appearing obstructionist, but nothing ultimately materialised.20

In the mid-late 1980s, the Soviets’ became far more willing to cooperate with the US under a newly-elected Gorbachev. For example, the Stockholm Document of 1986, signed by both parties, stated: “Aircraft for inspection will be chosen by mutual agreement between the inspecting and receiving States”. Gorbachev also played a key role in the subsequent INF treaty of 1987, which included inspections of nuclear facilities.

Gorbachev had indicated a commitment to Glasnost: openness and transparency in Soviet governance.21 This signalled a significant shift in Soviet international affairs policy.22 As Peter Jones — who was a part of Open Skies negotiations for the Canadian delegation, and an invaluable resource for this article — states in Open Skies: Transparency, Confidence-Building, and the End of the Cold War: “By the late 1980s the stage was thus set for a reconsideration of Open Skies. All that was required were the right circumstances and someone to give it a push.”23

In January 1989, President Bush ordered a National Security Directive for his national security team to conduct a wide-ranging review of initiatives they might take in response to the new geopolitical climate. Two of his advisors conceived of reviving Open Skies as a way that the US and its allies could respond to Gorbachev’s recent public relations victories.24

In May 1989, President Bush gave a public speech at Texas A&M University, publicly reviving the idea of open flights between the US and the Soviets.25 For the US, this meant an opportunity to test whether the discussion of Glasnost was substantive, or merely a public platitude. If the Soviets refused, this put the US in a strong position, where they could claim the Soviets were not committed to peace, where the US was.26

The Canadians’ desire to advance Open Skies played a vital role in bringing the treaty to fruition. The Canadians offered to organise, host, and pay all costs for the first conference, which took place in Ottawa.27 As Jones states: “the Canadian intervention appears to have been critical”.28

Through Canada’s urging, Open Skies was to include all NATO and Warsaw Pact nations.29 NATO and Warsaw states were very interested in the treaty, and were likely convinced by Canada’s argument that the treaty was a great opportunity for smaller states to monitor events in their neighbouring states, when they would not otherwise have the capability to do so.30

There was a significant feeling-out period from 1989-1990. The US was unsure how committed the Soviets were to Open Skies, and there was much discussion of Open Skies within the US, including within intelligence circles regarding its advantages and disadvantages.31

Before the first conference, the US outlined their initial positions to NATO allies, including:

The country conducting the overflight can use their own aircraft.

A notice period before arrival, with a flight plan to be considered upon arrival.

No restrictions on overflight territory, except those that applied to civilian aircraft.

No restrictions on sensors except for the banning of communications sensors.

Collected data would be the property of the overflying state.

Host-states could have their own observers present during overflights.

Increasing membership to the treaty would be possible.

Open Skies could be used for verification for other agreements, but had no explicit provisions within for doing so.

Allies could not overfly each other (as allies might use up each other’s overflight quota, thus other states would not be able to do overflights).32

Canada took the lead in drafting a text for NATO, which was discussed with the US. The US preferred to nail down concrete positions to then use for negotiations (and the Soviets were similar in this view), whereas the Canadians preferred to keep issues open for discussion.33

Unfortunately, NATO was unaware that the Soviets’ positions differed radically from theirs. The Soviets wanted a shared fleet of aircraft to be used for Open Skies. They also wanted all data to be processed centrally, and shared among treaty partners. Troublingly, the Soviets held that signatories’ bases in non-signatory states should be available for overflights under Open Skies (a position later admitted to be the Soviets stalling for time).34

A month before the Ottawa conference, on January 6th 1990, Canada and Hungary decided that Canada would conduct an overflight of Hungary to test whether short-notice flights were operationally possible. This was a strong success, and air traffic control was easily able to manage such flights, despite initial concerns of policymakers.35

The rush to enter into a conference instead of going through deeper pre-negotiations meant that negotiations likely happened far too early, before it was clear what the major issues were, and what positions each side held.36 There was so little time that the NATO position did not even become clear until the evening before official negotiations in Ottawa were to begin.37

Negotiations: 1990-1992

There were four formal rounds of negotiations before the final signing of the treaty in Helsinki, 1992. These were: Ottawa, February 1990; Budapest, April 1990; Vienna, November 1991; and Vienna (again), January 1992.38 Between Budapest and the first Vienna round, there was a one-and-a-half-year hiatus.39

Ottawa

The first Open Skies Conference was held in Ottawa, Canada on the 10th February 1990. Instead of discussing Open Skies, the start of the conference was focused largely on discussing the reunification of Germany.40 After this was out the way, Open Skies was up for discussion, based around the draft treaty crafted by Canada and the US.41

The Canadians, having paid for the conference, dictated much of the process of negotiation, focusing on large, formal discussions. This left little time for smaller discussions between states, in which states could informally discuss and negotiate serious differences in their positions.42

All parties agreed that communications were not to be monitored under the treaty.43 The Soviets, opposing the US, wanted open sharing of intelligence gathered, and lower optical resolution sensors. The Soviets also wanted host states to be able to choose whether the aircraft used for overflights would belong to the overflying country, a third party, or the overflown country. This was because they were afraid of hidden sensors on aircraft, and thus preferred their own aircraft be used over their territory.44 The US wanted sensors that could work in all weather and day or night, and the Soviets did not.45

Romania pushed back against the Soviets’ position of wanting overflights of non-signatory states who house bases of signatories in their territory. This kind of push-back was somewhat common in negotiations, where smaller states were willing to oppose policy positions they deemed unreasonable.46

Czechoslovakia proposed the “Grand Compromise” in Ottawa. This held that detailed imaging sensors of Western nations would be made available to all, raw data would be shared (at least between overflying and overflown nations), overflown nations would be able to use their own aircraft, there were compromises on quotas, full territorial overflights would be possible, and the USSR would drop its insistence on overflight of military bases in non-signatory states.47

Before Budapest, the US and USSR considered their positions in detail. The US still wanted to maintain some sensor advantage, and the Soviets wanted very weak sensors for everyone.48

Budapest

At Budapest, in April 1990, the Soviets conceded on using relatively strong 30cm optical resolution cameras as desired by the US, and synthetic aperture radar which could allow night and day monitoring in any weather. The US stated they were willing to “consider favorably requests for access to sensor systems”.49 Canada backed the Soviets to some degree in this exchange, where the US tried to maintain sensor advantages over other states.50

The Soviets had become willing to use US sensors installed on Soviet aircraft for overflights, although the Soviets only wanted to allow Soviet aircraft to do overflights of their territory.51 NATO, with the exception of the UK and US, largely wanted equal sensors.The US and UK quietly wanted to use superior sensors, and any data-sharing would compromise the fact that the equipment being used was unequal. The Soviets also wanted shared data and data processing between the host and overflying states. Many NATO members agreed that raw data at least ought to be shared, despite US and UK opposition.52

Flight quotas were heavily disputed. Many of the states present wanted to overfly the USSR, as opposed to other states. The Soviets continued to stick to their position of wanting overflights of signatory bases in non-signatory states.53

Foreshadowing a common theme, groups that worked on discussing more technical matters, such as mission regulations, air safety rules, transit flight regulations, and legal matters, made significant headway in a spirit of cooperation. However, many issues were not resolved, awaiting political agreement between the various states in order to make further progress.54

Ultimately, parties left Budapest with fairly divergent views. These issues were not insurmountable, but the US and USSR needed to reconsider their positions. Canada publicly criticised the US for wanting to use Open Skies as an intelligence mechanism, rather than a confidence building mechanism.55

Interim period

At the Bush-Gorbachev Summit May 30 - June 3 1990, there was a surprising amount of time spent discussing Open Skies. They identified which issues were contentious and thus required flexibility. NATO later released a joint statement in support of Open Skies, essentially pushing for the “Grand Compromise”.56

The US and NATO also wanted more intelligence around the Urals, concluding that an equal, cooperative, and only moderately intrusive Open Skies agreement was the only realistic way to achieve this.57 The US also changed its position on shared aircraft as a way forward, which was previously an avenue by which they could ensure superior sensing capabilities — a notable concession. However, this time the Soviets, potentially concerned about costs, backed away from their initial position.58 The end of the Cold War also brought an increased desire to influence world geopolitics.59

It was around one and a half years after Budapest before the next conference in Vienna. This delay was partly due to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, and the Gulf War in 1991.60

Vienna I

The US, UK, Germany, and France had been discussing Open Skies. It was not long into the Vienna conference in November 1991 that they presented a full draft treaty. March 1992 was reasonably proposed as a date for the signing of the treaty. The Soviet Ambassador Golovko stated at Vienna that: “We do not have any issues of principle which divide us. I believe that now we have a common approach.”61

Unlike previously, it was decided that there would be informal sessions, led by states with expertise in those areas, on various issues. These leaders often brought in technical experts to advance discussions about finer details to be used in a final version of the treaty.62

Cyprus’ potential inclusion in the treaty also came up as an issue, where the Turks were strongly opposed to Cyprus’ inclusion, and the Greeks were in favour. This was so divisive that it did not reach resolution, except that the expansion of the treaty would be addressed later.63

Sweden and Finland pushed for standard ground targets to be used for sensor calibration. This would ensure both that the US did not have sensors which were too advanced, and that the Soviets would not provide inadequate sensors. After some discussion, other states eventually agreed.64

Western European Union countries also found an alliance, particularly regarding pooling overflights together and sharing aircraft, given their limited amount of available aircraft, and the limited quota of overflights.65

Before the second round of negotiations in Vienna, the Soviet Union collapsed on 31 December 1991, and its place in Open Skies was taken by Russia.66 In this time, Canada also conducted a second overflight of Hungary, including over a nuclear facility, to test and demonstrate how overflights could be done with relative ease. This was a success, demonstrating that compromises on various issues were possible.67

Canada decided to reach out to former Soviet states about Open Skies. Ukraine and Belarus showed immediate interest in joining.68 Turkey signalled an interest in as many countries as possible being invited into the negotiation, except Cyprus.69

Vienna II

Various issues were discussed at Vienna II, occurring in January 1992, and many issues did not reach resolution. The French wanted the outcomes of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE) to play a significant role in Open Skies, but this opinion did not seem to be shared more widely.70 Russia wanted certain technical calibration techniques to be used for sensors which would effectively lead to lower sensor capabilities, but others were unwilling to accept this, and this issue was deferred.71 The US refused to pay costs when being forced to use Russian aircraft. However, some NATO countries were willing to pay costs such as fuel and lubricants. These costs were discussed in some detail, but were not fully resolved.72 It was decided that accession was contentious and would also be deferred, partly due to Cyprus.73

An Open Skies Consultative Commission (OSCC) was created to settle unresolved issues. The OSCC became the formal decision-making and negotiation body of the treaty, meeting four (or more, as needed) times per year, with their first meeting occurring nine days after the signing of the treaty.74 The OSCC consists of one delegate from each signatory, operates on the basis of consensus, and deals with amendments, cost-sharing, mission report handling, and changes to sensor capabilities, among other things.75

Some other issues were settled at Vienna II. It was decided that mission reports would be created before the exit of the observing party, signed by the observed party, and would be shared with all states parties within seven days of departure.76 Flight quotas were also resolved, where overflights received and conducted were roughly proportional to territorial area, although not all parties were satisfied.77 It was agreed that 42 overflights per year would be accepted by both the US and “the Republic of Belarus and the Russian Federation group of States Parties”, and 2-12 overflights per year for other states.78

Regarding notice periods, there would be 72 hours notice before a proposed flight, with 24 hours to acknowledge that notice and whether the host will provide aircraft. Flight plans would be given over for inspection upon arrival. The host had four hours after receiving the flight plan to suggest changes for flight safety reasons, 24 hours from arrival until the flight occurs, 24 hours to leave after the flight (unless safety was a concern).79

Implementation and decline: 1992-2021

The Treaty on Open Skies was signed by 25 nations on 24 March 1992 in Helsinki. It came into effect on January 1 2002, after it was ratified by 20 state parties, delayed by the ratification of Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine.80 In this time, the OSCC agreed on issues that were deferred, such as technical sensor capabilities and accession, where the OSCC were allowed to approve accession applications after the treaty came into force.81

Russia delayed their ratification for several reasons: there were other areas of focus; Russia was concerned about the value of what it was gaining from the treaty given Western advantages; and costs were significant, since Russia preferred their own aircraft being used for overflights of their own territory.82 However, after some time, it was realised that dwindling satellite resources meant that Russia could gain significant intelligence on the West through Open Skies at comparable costs to satellites. An internal memo stated: “[We] can conclude that the Treaty on Open Skies is advantageous to Russia, and allows for some compensation of Western superiority in obtaining information with minimal expenditures.”83

Between 1992 and 2000, the OSCC had made 22 binding decisions. Overflights were common, with over 400 before 2002, even though the treaty had not yet come into effect.84 Aircraft and sensors were prepared, including targets used for calibration, and verifying calibration.85

Initial sensor-certification of aircraft occurred from 1997-2002. The aircraft used for Open Skies (as of 2004) belonged to ten states (Bulgaria, Czech Rep., Hungary, Romania, Russia, Sweden, Turkey, Ukraine, UK, USA), plus the “Pod Group” (Belgium, Canada, France, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain).86 Certification events were held, with a length of up to seven days per aircraft to be certified, and 60 days’ prior notice. These events allowed up to four participants per signatory state to be involved (though the certifying state could limit total participants to 40). Certification included flights with at least five passes over on-ground certification targets.

The first certification event occurred in 1997 for German aircraft, which easily reached the maximum capacity of 40 participants. Following this, there were successful certification events in 2000 and 2001, in which multiple states brought their aircraft to the events for certification.87 In December 2001, the OSCC decided that there would be a seven-month certification period for aircraft and sensors from 1 January 2002 to 31 July 2002. There were four certification events in this period, in which many aircraft were certified.88 All observed states also have a right to conduct pre-flight inspection of aircraft and sensors to check for tampering and resolution requirements, and observed states are always aboard the aircraft during overflights.89

After ratification, many European states were admitted to Open Skies, as were Georgia and Kyrgyzstan. Turkey continued to object to the inclusion of Cyprus.90 Eventually, in 2011, after continued mention of Cyprus from other states, Turkey blocked any mention of Cyprus in the OSCC agenda, effectively stopping Cyprus from ever entering the treaty.91

Open Skies was also used as a vehicle for territorial disputes. In 2010 the US and Romania requested a flight near Russia's border with Georgia, which the Russians rejected on the grounds that the flight was too near a border with a state — “Abkhazia” — which was not a party to the treaty (and which the US did not recognise).92

From 2014 to 2020, tensions rose between the US and Russia regarding Russia’s annexation of Crimea, and Russia’s tensions with Ukraine.93

The United States left Open Skies in 2020, citing numerous Russian violations of the treaty, disagreements over the status of Crimea and other territories, and broader patterns of mistrust.94 Russia then left in 2021, citing unwarranted sharing of treaty data to non-signatory states, US withdrawal, disinclination towards US arms control (including Biden reaffirming the the Trump administration’s decision to leave Open Skies), and the refusal of European states to allow overflights of US military facilities within their state.95 Given the war between Russia and Ukraine, agreements such as Open Skies and the CFE may be beyond repair.96

Thirty-two states currently remain in the Treaty on Open Skies: Canada, Kyrgyzstan, and 30 European nations.97 There is some thought that Open Skies could still be useful in its current capacity — even in the absence of the US and Russia — for things like arms control, military-military discussion, and for verifying other agreements, with the potential for expansion of inspected territories.98

Contentious issues in negotiation

This section examines five major issues that shaped negotiations. It shows how different states approached key issues, what motivated their positions, and what lessons these conflicts offer.

Issue 1: Sensor capabilities

Throughout negotiations the US, with the backing of the UK, wanted to use their higher-capability sensors to have a sensor advantage over the Soviets. The Soviets wanted low-resolution sensors, and initially were against all-weather and day-and-night monitoring using synthetic-aperture radar (SAR). Eventually it was agreed that there would be equal sensor capabilities with moderate-high sensing capabilities, all-party calibration events to ensure compliance with agreed OSCC standards, and sharing of sensors to middle powers.

The journey to agreement on sensors is multifaceted. When Bush first ordered his National Security Directive in 1989, there was considerable internal discussion of relevant tradeoffs between openness and security, and thus sensing capabilities.Those in the US typically charged with collection of data were in favour of more capable sensors to gain intelligence on the Soviet Union, thinking that the US had much more to gain from inspection than the Soviets. Those concerned with protecting intelligence data were more cautious, and were particularly worried about the prospect of US communications being intercepted, pushing for large no-fly areas. No-fly areas were opposed by Canada, and eventually this position was rejected in favour of more openness.99

All parties agreed early that communications would not be monitored under the Open Skies.100 The Soviets, afraid of hidden sensors, preferred their own aircraft or shared aircraft to be used in their territory. All other states were prepared to allow overflying countries to use their own aircraft.101 The US initially wanted sensors that could work in all weather and day or night (SAR), and the Soviets pushed for low-resolution optical sensors and no SAR, eventually suggesting very low-capability SAR with 10m resolution. Finally, in Budapest, the Soviets conceded on using 30cm optical resolution cameras and 3m resolution SAR, as desired by the US and NATO.102 The US, responding to middle powers’ desires for using good sensor technology and equal sensors, became willing to “consider favorably requests for access to sensor systems”.103

One issue brought up by Finland and Sweden during Vienna I was that SAR sensors had a wider field of view than other sensors, potentially leading to data gathering of non-signatory territories, which also conflicted with Finnish law. Eventually it was agreed that aircraft would not be used within 10km of a border of a non-signatory state, and there was a preamble of the treaty which specified an intent to observe only one state party.104 The Finns and Swedes, fearing the Soviets trying to lower sensor capabilities, also pushed for using on-ground sensor calibration targets to ensure capabilities, and eventually persuaded others.105

After signing in 1992, the OSCC made their final decisions on technical capabilities of sensors. For example, optical cameras were deemed to be “calibrated” if they had resolution of between 25mm and 35mm in various conditions, such as atmospheric changes.106 Certification events would involve all signatory states that wanted to attend, and sensors could be inspected by an overflown nation to ensure calibration before an overflight.107

Issue 2: Costs

Costs proved contentious despite being relatively modest. The main expenses included aircraft, sensors, personnel, and overflight operations. Middle powers strongly preferred shared aircraft or to use the aircraft of other nations, as they did not easily have the resources/budget to build their own. In Vienna I, Russia, adamant that its own aircraft be used for overflights of its territory, insisted other nations pay some costs for the use of these aircraft. Much of NATO was willing to pay for fuel and lubricants, however the US was not, and Russia did not budge from their position.108

Cost issues took many years to resolve through the OSCC, with some resolutions occurring as late as 2009. The observing party using their own aircraft would cover local expenditures such as refuelling or servicing, reimbursing the observed party. Similarly, the observing party using the aircraft of the observed party would cover costs of fuel, services, etc. for the host’s aircraft. And if the observing party used a third party’s aircraft, reimbursement would be “fair and reasonable and be established in accordance with the arrangements of the States Parties concerned”.109

How costs influenced states’ decision-making is discussed in the Lessons learned section.

Issue 3: Formal discussions did not resolve all issues

Canada’s strict dictation of the processes of the Ottawa and Hungary conferences led to significant frustration that there was far too little time for informal discussions to happen, where the heart of issues could be addressed. This was rectified in the Vienna rounds, where there was far more room for informal discussions to happen, and those leading discussions often had technical expertise available to assist discussion.

Issue 4: Who owns the overflying aircraft?

There was considerable debate around the issue of which aircraft would be used in Open Skies overflights. Mainly, the Soviets/Russia were concerned that there would be sensors hidden in aircraft, and thus insisted on an option where the host’s aircraft could be used in overflights of their own territory.110 For the US, there were concerns that sensors aboard Russian aircraft would be considerably weaker than their own.111

These concerns were eventually resolved by ensuring that sensors on all Open Skies aircraft be carefully calibrated, that the overflown state could choose whether their own aircraft be used, and that the host and the overflying crew would work together during overflights.112

Issue 5: Accession and disputed territories

Throughout negotiations, all parties were broadly in favour of including other states in the treaty, including former Soviet states. However, one issue which caused significant tension was the inclusion of Cyprus. Turkey, not recognising the statehood of Cyprus, was insistent throughout negotiations that Cyprus not join Open Skies. Greece especially pushed back against Turkey. After continual mention of Cyprus in the proceedings of the OSCC by other states, in 2011 Turkey blocked all mention of Cyprus in OSCC discussions, essentially ending the possibility of Cyprus’ inclusion in Open Skies.113

Otherwise, treaty accession was relatively open. Canada’s initial choice to bring smaller European nations into discussions was one of the most influential aspects of accession. These states strengthened the veracity of negotiations, often bringing issues forward when there might otherwise have been insurmountable disputes between the US and the Soviets/Russia.114 The quick inclusion of former Soviet States after the fall of the USSR also supported negotiations, both because the Warsaw Treaty members had significant commonality, and because they were willing to push back against Russia when they thought Russian positions were unreasonable.

In 2010, the US and Romania deliberately requested a flight path near Georgia's border, creating a territorial dispute. Russia rejected the request, claiming the path was too close to "Abkhazia" — a territory Russia recognized but other signatories did not.115

Lessons learned

This section discusses lessons learned from Open Skies for future international agreements.

Lesson 1: There are several structural treaty elements of Open Skies which led to its success

Concrete elements of the treaty enabled Open Skies to satisfy all treaty parties, such that Open Skies lasted well for almost 30 years, before the US left in 2020 and Russia followed soon after in 2021. These elements are:

Short-notice overflights (72 hours) with inspection/flight plans given to the overflown state at least 24 hours before the overflight is to take place.

Overflight access to the entire territory of signatories, bar some safety/logistical exceptions, but with no exceptions for intelligence or secrecy reasons

Cooperative certification events for aircraft and sensors.

Equality of sensors.

Pre-flight inspections of aircraft, if requested by the host state.

Cooperation during missions between overflying and overflown states.

Detailed missions reports containing key inspection findings sent to all signatory states after each inspection, signed-off by the overflown state.

Availability of all raw mission data, upon request by signatories.

Some cost-sharing, including aircraft-sharing and sensor-sharing from better-resourced states, or pooling of resources by smaller states, and reimbursement by the overflying state to the overflown state for mission expenses.

The creation of the Open Skies Consultative Commission (OSCC): a treaty body with a representative from each signatory state to resolve disputes and make future decisions about Open Skies. The commission operated on the basis of consensus, and met at least four times per year.

Future verification agreements could do well to consider and potentially include, in their own context, many or all of these elements which allowed Open Skies to flourish.

Lesson 2: Middle powers can be decisive facilitators in negotiations

Apart from the US and USSR/Russia, Canada’s involvement played the most significant role in Open Skies coming to fruition. Not only did Canada organise and pay for the entire first conference, they also strongly pushed the US and NATO to adopt Open Skies from the outset, brought in European nations, coordinated two test overflights with Hungary to prove the possibility of Open Skies overflights, and were very active throughout negotiations in trying to articulate and resolve issues.

Other middle powers had significant impacts too. Finland, Sweden, Romania, Germany, France, the UK, Turkey, Spain, Italy, and others all were deeply involved in moving forward negotiation. Their positioning allowed them to call out hypocrisy, secrecy of intention, and unrealistic positioning where they were present. NATO was also significant in forming their positions and bringing forward draft texts for discussion.

“High-level involvement by the most powerful European allies was crucial in pressuring the U.S. bureaucracy to move in new directions and in forging the final compromises. The growing interest of the Europeans was motivated by a realisation that Open Skies would enable them to independently monitor events outside of the CFE verification zone.”116

Lesson 3: Commitment from a major power is essential

Open Skies succeeded only because of political will from US and Soviet leadership, with the US leading the initiative.

In 1989, Bush made a significant high-level commitment to Open Skies. The Presidential initiative to pursue Open Skies was largely followed, and difficult to oppose internally.117 The US sustained its commitment throughout negotiations, even when progress stalled. The extended break between Budapest and Vienna I allowed both superpowers to reassess their strategies. Although Canada pushed negotiations forward, they could not have done this without commitment from the US.118 Jones claims that agreements like Open Skies must be led by the US.119

The Soviets’ commitment to Glasnost was also pivotal. Although the Soviets first thought Open Skies was a Western intelligence ploy, they had already publicly declared a desire for peace and transparency, and may have genuinely held these desires. Their significant skepticism of the West meant that they were trepidatious throughout negotiations, but still maintained their involvement. Bush’s meeting with Gorbachev in 1990 allowed the US and USSR to see eye-to-eye on many issues. Eventually, Russia signed Open Skies after seeing its advantages.

Lesson 4: Equality and proportional treatment can be inevitable negotiation endpoints

Throughout negotiations, the US wanted to maintain advantages over other states, particularly the Soviets. However, the final treaty featured considerable equality between parties. Three key aspects demonstrated this equality: equal sensors, proportional overflight quotas based on territorial area, and equal access to mission reports and data.

This shift toward equality resulted from three factors. First, middle powers played a significant role. As smaller nations, they wanted maximum influence over the treaty and its implementation. Second, the initial US and Soviet positions proved unacceptable to other parties, meaning middle powers often encouraged both superpowers to change their stances. Third, equal treatment proved more palatable to most states than alternatives that favoured the major powers.

If negotiators had focused on equal treatment from the start, they could have saved considerable time and avoided extensive power struggles. Open Skies remained beneficial to the major powers even with equal treatment provisions. Both the US and Russia eventually recognised that equality served their interests, though this realisation took time. For future agreements, negotiators should consider establishing equality and proportionality as core principles early in the process rather than as eventual compromises.

Lesson 5: Domestic and geopolitical factors play a significant role in shaping negotiations

The political circumstances of the time — nearing the end of the Cold War, and the fall of the Soviet Union — were significant for Open Skies. The Soviets had good reason to want peace, and Open Skies was a mechanism for this. The US wanted to be a dominant player in the new geopolitical landscape, and wanted confidence that the Soviets were not involved in building up military capabilities beyond the Yurals. Open Skies was an excellent vehicle for these goals, giving the US significant influence, and providing intelligence beyond that which could be gathered by other means, such as infrequent or patchy satellite data.

Canada and the other middle powers saw Open Skies as a vehicle to be further involved in international politics, and as a way to monitor different territories.120 The focus from middle powers on wanting to be treated equally throughout negotiations also played an important role in agreed verification mechanisms, meaning it became no longer feasible for the US to want to maintain a sensor advantage. This led to access to all data, and equality of sensors and aircraft. The involvement of middle powers also likely influenced the structure of the OSCC, which operated on the basis of consensus, and each state was on equal footing.

Political priorities had shifted from the late 2000s onwards, eventually leading to the US leaving Open Skies in 2020, and Russia in 2021. With the ongoing war in Ukraine and relevant territorial disputes, it seems neither the US or Russia are interested in Open Skies anymore.

Lesson 6: States resist intrusive verification when they perceive unfair treatment and distrust

Invasive verification requires a level of trust, which can be supported by treaty elements. Cooperation between states, such as during mission overflights, and equal treatment in verification mechanisms, became vital keys to overcoming hesitancies about such verification. Hesitancies were heightened by states vying for advantages, such as when the US and UK secretly wanted to use superior sensors. Progress was made only when states were willing to embrace cooperation. Specifically, this cooperation came in the form of fairness in joint certification of aircraft and sensors, standardised sensor capabilities, shared inspection data, and direct coordination between host and overflying states.

As Jones states: “Cooperation (in mission operations), Equality (in sensors), and Sharing (in sensor capabilities and overflight results) are what might be called the “Golden Rules” of Open Skies. Allowing another state to perform a surveillance overflight is one of the most dramatic concessions a state can make in terms of its sovereignty. No state will do so unless the flights are done in a cooperative manner; done on the basis of equality; and the results are shared.”121

Lesson 7: Establishing shared goals before establishing mechanisms could accelerate negotiations

Jones maintains that one of the most important aspects to get right in agreements like Open Skies is to have clear agreement on the goals of the treaty.122 This was not done well in the beginnings of Open Skies. When both goals and the mechanisms by which they are to be accomplished were negotiated at the same time, it was difficult to make meaningful progress. Explicitly, parties should lay out the problem(s) the agreement is trying to solve, and what exact solutions it proposes.

There were many instances throughout negotiations where disagreements occurred because goals were unclear.123 For example, was Open Skies about equal sensing capabilities of all parties during overflights, or states using near-unlimited sensory capabilities over other state territories? Was it about cooperative confidence-building through open sharing of data, or about strategic intelligence gathering for each individual state?

Although agreements like Open Skies will always have incentives towards gaining strategic advantage, if its purposes were clear, this could have saved a lot of time and difficulty. Thus, goals should be discussed as explicitly as possible early in negotiations before pushing for verification mechanisms that may be based on entirely different goals. This is not to say that negotiating and agreeing on goals is easy, or that goals and mechanisms are entirely distinct from each other. Rather, where goals and mechanisms were mixed in Open Skies, and states were also pushing for strategic advantages, negotiating goals first could have considerably decreased many of the frictions that occurred.

Lesson 8: Different negotiation formats serve different purposes, and all can be useful

Productive negotiations can arise through many different formats, and each has their own advantages. These can range from formal, process-based negotiations, to leader-leader discussions such as the Bush-Gorbachev meeting in 1990, to informal positional discussions, to allied discussions and treaty drafting, such as that which occurred with NATO, to pre-negotiations. Technical discussions and consultation can also be vital and time-saving. All of these different types of negotiations had their place in Open Skies.

Formal discussions, such as those that occurred in Ottawa and Budapest, can mean that all parties are involved and informed, and can be good for stating firm positions. However, these can also mean that underlying issues do not get addressed. The rigidity and formality of early Open Skies negotiations is one of the reasons that negotiations stalled: state parties did not have informal settings in which they could clearly stake out their positions and argue their case at the deepest levels.

The Bush-Gorbachev meeting involved much unplanned discussion about Open Skies. Leader-leader discussions can be invaluable for rapport-building, clearly and openly stating one’s positions and responding, and furthering negotiations.

Informal discussions are extremely useful in allowing state parties to consider the perspectives of another, to clarify areas of disagreement, and to negotiate a path to agreement.

Allied discussions can bring clarity to positions. They can also inform and support the production of draft texts, which can considerably move processes along. Allies can prioritise which issues they are willing to negotiate, and which they will stay firm on.

Pre-negotiations can also be extremely useful. Arguably, not enough pre-negotiation occurred in Ottawa, which meant that states came in with radically different positions, unaware of the positions of others. In particular, the US and USSR were quite unaware of the others’ positions, and therefore which issues would be contentious. Deeper investment into pre-negotiations could avoid these difficulties.124

Lastly, technical discussions can resolve issues that might otherwise seem very difficult. At the first Vienna conference, the UK, having noticed unhappiness with the previous working group structure and the value of informal communications, suggested that there be small, informal sessions led by individuals. There were various groups. The UK led discussion on sensors with a sensor expert present. Germany led operational questions. France led legal issues. The US took over consideration of a range of relevant texts for the treaty such as definitions. Canada hosted discussions on the preamble and Article 1. The expertise of these groups was very useful in establishing drafts which contained considerable technical detail, rather than leaving much of this up for discussion and later negotiation. This simplified negotiations considerably, and provided much more useful focus for discussions.125 There were many other useful inclusions of technical expertise. Technical cooperation between the overflying and overflown nation’s teams was necessary for coordination of overflights. When consulted, air traffic control saw no issues with what were considered to be very short-notice flights, which was previously a considerable worry. Bodies such as the OSCC were able to use technical expertise to resolve various problems, such as defining a useful range of optical sensor capability.

Lesson 9: Costs can play a significant part in confidence-building agreements

Costs became a significant issue at various times throughout Open Skies negotiations. Governments have limited budgets, and often arms control is not a priority, meaning funding can be limited.126

There are many relevant examples of cost issues. Early in Open Skies, US intelligence did not want costs to be covered under their budget unless there were significant intelligence advances.127 Costs were also a significant point of discussion with NATO members before Ottawa.128 Costs became an issue when, after the Soviets had pushed for shared aircraft, the US changed their position, but by 1991 Moscow no longer had the budget to contribute, or may have been partly showing their lack of interest in Open Skies at the time.129 Later, at Vienna I, the Soviets disputed that they should bear the costs of overflights of their territory if their aircraft were used.130 Costs also played into the sensor debate, where the US tied the sensor issue to the cost issue, as something to be deferred for the OSCC. The US continued to not want to pay for the use of Russia’s aircraft, whereas other NATO members were willing to pay for expenses such as fuel and lubricants.131 Only in 2001 did Russia consider Open Skies’ costs palatable, when it was realised that the costs of intelligence gathered from Open Skies were comparable to intelligence gains by other means.132 Costs took a long time to be fully resolved through the OSCC, where it was eventually agreed that observing states would bear most costs.133

Conclusion

This article has given an overview of the historical aspects of Open Skies, discussed the most contentious issues and reasons for contention, and drawn valuable lessons.

Particularly contentious issues in Open Skies were: sensor capabilities, costs, negotiation formats, aircraft ownership, and accession and territories.

Key lessons learned from Open Skies were: there are several structural treaty elements of Open Skies which led to its success; middle powers can be decisive facilitators in negotiations; commitment from a major power is essential; equality and proportional treatment can be inevitable negotiation endpoints; domestic and geopolitical factors play a significant role in shaping negotiations; states resist intrusive verification when they perceive unfair treatment and distrust; establishing shared goals before establishing mechanisms could accelerate negotiations; different negotiation formats serve different purposes, and all can be useful; and costs can play a significant part in confidence-building agreements.

These lessons will apply to different types of agreements in different ways, and could be used to inform future international agreements, such as an international AI verification agreement.
